title: Don't be angry: la taghdab
hookLine: a man asks for advice, and is told three times: don't be angry (Nawawi 16, Abu Hurayrah)
carry: la taghdab: feel the heat, don't act from it
tomorrow: why does a hadith about excellence mention sharpening a blade?

lines: A GROUP CHAT, A VOICE MEMO.
cards: A man asks for advice and gets two words. Why say them again? Ask a group chat for advice and you get paragraphs, links, a voice memo.
In al-Nawawi's sixteenth hadith, a man comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and says: advise me. The answer: don't be angry. He asks again.
Don't be angry. He keeps asking, and the answer doesn't move. Not a speech.
Not a plan. That's the odd detail. Why so small?

teach.b: The hadith is in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by Abu Hurayrah. In Arabic the answer is two words: la taghdab. Look at what the man is doing.
He wants more: a second tip, a bigger one, something that sounds like wisdom. And the answer refuses to grow.

teach.h: HOW DO YOU NOT FEEL IT?
teach.b: Some readers take that as the first lesson: the advice that fits you isn't always the advice you'd have picked. He may have hoped for something lofty. He got something he could use before lunch.
Then the puzzle inside the puzzle. Anger arrives on its own. How can anyone be told not to have a feeling?

teach.h: DON'T ACT FROM IT. BUILD THE BRAKE.
teach.b: One: don't act from it. The heat may come; the words and the slammed door don't have to follow. Two: become a person who isn't easily set off, which is slow work, done one morning at a time.

teach.h: STANDING? SIT. STILL ANGRY? LIE DOWN.
teach.b: Another hadith gives the body a part in it: if anger hits while you're standing, sit down; if it stays, lie down. Lower the body, and the heat often comes down too. It's advice for a body, not only a mind.
And the Qur'an praises those who hold back their anger and pardon people. Hold back, not erase. The feeling may come into the room.
It just doesn't get the keys.

how: Muslims often quote 'la taghdab' to each other in heated moments, and some follow the hadith's advice literally, sitting down, making wudu, or seeking refuge in Allah when anger rises.

o: not letting anger make your choices
showing anger openly, never hiding it
never once feeling irritated at all

games.q: the man and the answer — tap the pairs.
p: the man's request, again and again

s: the hadith means you sin just by feeling angry
it's usually read as: don't act from it, and grow a character that's slow to ignite.
the man asked more than once and got the same answer
he kept asking, and it stayed: don't be angry.
another hadith advises sitting down when anger hits while standing
and if it stays, lying down. lower the body, lower the heat.

games.q: your little brother breaks your headphones and laughs. you're shaking. by today's hadith, what comes first?
o: sit down, breathe, and let it cool before you speak.
tell him calmly you're not angry, even though you are.
let it all out now so it doesn't build up later.
games.why: 'don't be angry' with the sit-down hadith: the feeling may come; you lower the body before the words go out.

practice: Take the posture from that hadith on purpose. If you're standing, sit; if you're sitting, drop your shoulders and rest your hands open on your knees.
Bring to mind one thing that got under your skin lately, and on each out-breath let the body get a little lower and slower than the thought.

wordCard.voice: Don't be angry: la taghdab, two words in Arabic. The man asked for more, and the answer stayed exactly these two, every time.

orig.note: Arabic: don't be angry, from ghadab, anger. The whole answer, two words long.

carryVoice: For the road: la taghdab. Feel the heat, don't act from it; a hand on the door anger wants to slam. Hadith sixteen, done.

sources.ref: al-Nawawi, al-Arba'in, hadith 16; Sahih al-Bukhari 6116 (Abu Hurayrah)
Sunan Abu Dawud 4782 (Abu Dharr: if angry while standing, sit; if it stays, lie down)
Qur'an 3:134 (those who hold back anger and pardon people)
